items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll extend our knowledge of gradients of scalar-valued functions.

Content:
Recall that, for a function [MATH: f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}] that maps a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] to a scalar value [MATH: f(\mathbf{x})], the gradient of [MATH: f] with respect to [MATH: \mathbf{x}] is defined as the column vector of partial derivatives:

Content:
[MATH: [(∂f)/(∂x_{1}); (∂f)/(∂x_{2}); ⋮; (∂f)/(∂x_{n})]]

Content:
Note: Some resources use [MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf x}] to denote the gradient. We shall avoid this notation.

Content:
Recall that the total derivative of a scalar function [MATH: f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}] with respect to a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] is the row vector

Content:
[MATH: [(∂f)/(∂x_{1})|(∂f)/(∂x_{2})|⋯|(∂f)/(∂x_{n})]]

Content:
Hence, the gradient is simply the transpose of the total derivative:

Content:
[MATH: \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \left( \frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T]

Content:
We'll now discuss some important results related to gradients widely used in machine learning applications.

Content:
Let's see an example.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let’s derive a general rule for the gradient of a linear function.

Content:
Suppose [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n,] and the scalar function [MATH: f] is given by
[MATH: f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x},]
where [MATH: \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^n] is a fixed vector.

Content:
We wish to find an expression for the gradient of [MATH: f.]
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x})]

Content:
To do this, let's write our vectors [MATH: \mathbf b] and [MATH: \mathbf x] explicitly:

Content:
[MATH: [b_{1}; b_{2}; ⋮; b_{n}]]

Content:
Then, [MATH: \mathbf b^T \mathbf x] is the scalar function
[MATH: b^{T}x|= [b_{1}|b_{2}|…|b_{n}][x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]]
which simplifies as
[MATH: \mathbf b^T \mathbf x
=b_1x_1+ b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_nx_n.]

Content:
The partial derivative of [MATH: \mathbf b^T \mathbf x] with respect to [MATH: x_i] is [MATH: b_i,] since all the other terms will vanish.
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(\mathbf b^T\mathbf x\right) = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(b_1x_1+ b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_i x_i + \cdots + b_nx_n\right) = b_i]

Content:
Since this is true for all [MATH: 1\leq i\leq n,] we have
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf x} \left(\mathbf b^T \mathbf x\right) = \mathbf b]
as required.

Content:
This is the multivariable analog of the familiar rule from single-variable calculus:

Content:
[MATH: \frac{\textrm d}{\textrm dx}(a x) = a]

Content:
We have the following result:

Content:
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf w} \left(\mathbf w^T \mathbf w\right) = 2\mathbf w]

Content:
This result is analogous to the following result from single-variable calculus:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d w}(w^2) = 2w]

Content:
To see why this is true, let [MATH: \mathbf w \in\mathbb R^n] be given by
[MATH: [w_{1}; w_{2}; ⋮; w_{n}]]

Content:
Then, [MATH: \mathbf w^T \mathbf w] is the scalar function
[MATH: w^{T}w|= [w_{1}|w_{2}|…|w_{n}][w_{1}; w_{2}; ⋮; w_{n}]]
which can be written as
[MATH: \mathbf w^T \mathbf w
=w_1^2+ w_2^2 + \cdots + w_n^2.]
The partial derivative of [MATH: \mathbf w^T \mathbf w] with respect to [MATH: w_i] is [MATH: 2w_i,] since all the other terms will vanish. Since this is true for all [MATH: 1\leq i\leq n,] we have
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf w} \left(\mathbf w^T \mathbf w\right) = 2\mathbf w]
as required.

Content:
Finally, note that since

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf w^T \mathbf w = ||\mathbf w ||^2]
we have the following equivalent result:

Content:
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf w}(||\mathbf w ||^2) = 2\mathbf w]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll extend our knowledge of gradients of scalar-valued functions.

Content:
Recall that, for a function [MATH: f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}] that maps a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] to a scalar value [MATH: f(\mathbf{x})], the gradient of [MATH: f] with respect to [MATH: \mathbf{x}] is defined as the column vector of partial derivatives:

Content:
[MATH: [(∂f)/(∂x_{1}); (∂f)/(∂x_{2}); ⋮; (∂f)/(∂x_{n})]]

Content:
Note: Some resources use [MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf x}] to denote the gradient. We shall avoid this notation.

Content:
Recall that the total derivative of a scalar function [MATH: f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}] with respect to a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] is the row vector

Content:
[MATH: [(∂f)/(∂x_{1})|(∂f)/(∂x_{2})|⋯|(∂f)/(∂x_{n})]]

Content:
Hence, the gradient is simply the transpose of the total derivative:

Content:
[MATH: \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \left( \frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T]

Content:
We'll now discuss some important results related to gradients widely used in machine learning applications.

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Gradient of a Linear Form With Respect to a Vector

Content:
Let’s derive a general rule for the gradient of a linear function.

Content:
Suppose [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n,] and the scalar function [MATH: f] is given by
[MATH: f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x},]
where [MATH: \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^n] is a fixed vector.

Content:
We wish to find an expression for the gradient of [MATH: f.]
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x})]

Content:
To do this, let's write our vectors [MATH: \mathbf b] and [MATH: \mathbf x] explicitly:

Content:
[MATH: [b_{1}; b_{2}; ⋮; b_{n}]]

Content:
Then, [MATH: \mathbf b^T \mathbf x] is the scalar function
[MATH: b^{T}x|= [b_{1}|b_{2}|…|b_{n}][x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]]
which simplifies as
[MATH: \mathbf b^T \mathbf x
=b_1x_1+ b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_nx_n.]

Content:
The partial derivative of [MATH: \mathbf b^T \mathbf x] with respect to [MATH: x_i] is [MATH: b_i,] since all the other terms will vanish.
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(\mathbf b^T\mathbf x\right) = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(b_1x_1+ b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_i x_i + \cdots + b_nx_n\right) = b_i]

Content:
Since this is true for all [MATH: 1\leq i\leq n,] we have
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf x} \left(\mathbf b^T \mathbf x\right) = \mathbf b]
as required.

Content:
This is the multivariable analog of the familiar rule from single-variable calculus:

Content:
[MATH: \frac{\textrm d}{\textrm dx}(a x) = a]

---

Item 3 — Example: Computing Gradients of Linear Forms

Example Prompt:
Compute the gradient of the function [MATH: f: \mathbb{R}^4 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}] defined by [MATH: [0|1|0|− 1]] with respect to [MATH: \mathbf{x}] at [MATH: [1; 0; 1; 0]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Writing [MATH: [0; 1; 0; − 1]], we have
[MATH: f(\mathbf{x})= \mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{x}.]

The gradient of a function [MATH: f(x) = \mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{x}] with respect to [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] is
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}.]
Therefore, we get
[MATH: [0; 1; 0; − 1]]

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Gradient of a Squared Norm

Content:
We have the following result:

Content:
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf w} \left(\mathbf w^T \mathbf w\right) = 2\mathbf w]

Content:
This result is analogous to the following result from single-variable calculus:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d w}(w^2) = 2w]

Content:
To see why this is true, let [MATH: \mathbf w \in\mathbb R^n] be given by
[MATH: [w_{1}; w_{2}; ⋮; w_{n}]]

Content:
Then, [MATH: \mathbf w^T \mathbf w] is the scalar function
[MATH: w^{T}w|= [w_{1}|w_{2}|…|w_{n}][w_{1}; w_{2}; ⋮; w_{n}]]
which can be written as
[MATH: \mathbf w^T \mathbf w
=w_1^2+ w_2^2 + \cdots + w_n^2.]
The partial derivative of [MATH: \mathbf w^T \mathbf w] with respect to [MATH: w_i] is [MATH: 2w_i,] since all the other terms will vanish. Since this is true for all [MATH: 1\leq i\leq n,] we have
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf w} \left(\mathbf w^T \mathbf w\right) = 2\mathbf w]
as required.

Content:
Finally, note that since

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf w^T \mathbf w = ||\mathbf w ||^2]
we have the following equivalent result:

Content:
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf w}(||\mathbf w ||^2) = 2\mathbf w]

---

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the results
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf w}(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}, \qquad \nabla_{\mathbf w} (\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{w}) = 2\mathbf{w},]
we have

[MATH: ∇_{w}f|= ∇_{w}(− 7w^{T}x + 3‖w‖^{2} − 2); = − 7 ⋅ ∇_{w}(w^{T}x) + 3 ⋅ ∇_{w}(‖w‖^{2}) − ∇_{w}(2); = − 7 ⋅ ∇_{w}(w^{T}x) + 3 ⋅ ∇_{w}(w^{T}w) − ∇_{w}(2); = − 7 ⋅ x + 3 ⋅ 2w − 0; = − 7x + 6w.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: The Gradient of the L1 Norm

Content:
Consider the [MATH: \textrm{L}_1] (Manhattan) norm of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n], defined as
[MATH: \|\mathbf{x}\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|.]

Content:
We want to compute the gradient of this function with respect to [MATH: \mathbf{x}]. To do that, let’s focus on finding the partial derivative with respect to a single component [MATH: x_k{:}]

Content:
[MATH: (∂‖x‖_{1})/(∂x_{k})|= (∂)/(∂x_{k})∑_(i = 1)^(n)|x_{i}|; = (∂)/(∂x_{k})(|x_{1}|+|x_{2}|+ ⋯ +|x_{k}|+ ⋯ +|x_{n}|); = (∂|x_{1}|)/(∂x_{k}) + (∂|x_{2}|)/(∂x_{k}) + ⋯ + (∂|x_{k}|)/(∂x_{k}) + ⋯ + (∂|x_{n}|)/(∂x_{k}); = (∂|x_{k}|)/(∂x_{k}); = sign(x_{k}),]

Content:
where [MATH: \text{sign}(x_k)] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: {−1,|x_{k} > 0,; − 1,|x_{k} < 0.]

Content:
So, the full gradient of the [MATH: \textrm{L}_1] norm is simply
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \|\mathbf{x}\|_1 = \text{sign}(\mathbf{x}),]
which is a vector whose [MATH: k]th component is [MATH: \text{sign}(x_k)].

Content:
The gradient of [MATH: \|\mathbf x\|_1] is not defined at points where any component of [MATH: \mathbf x] equals zero. This is because the absolute value function has a sharp corner at zero and is therefore not differentiable there. Various methods are available to overcome this difficulty when the derivative of the [MATH: \textrm L1] norm is used in practice, and we'll discuss these in future lessons.

---

Item 11 — Tutorial: Chain Rule to Vector Gradients

Content:
In many machine learning models, a scalar function depends on a vector that itself depends on another vector.

Content:
Suppose [MATH: f:\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}] and [MATH: \mathbf g:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m,] and define
[MATH: h(\mathbf x)=f(\mathbf g(\mathbf x)).]

Content:
Then the chain rule for gradients states:
[MATH: \nabla_{\mathbf x} h(\mathbf x)
=
J_{\mathbf g}(\mathbf x)^T
\,\nabla_{\mathbf u} f(\mathbf u)\Big|_{\mathbf u=\mathbf g(\mathbf x)},]
where [MATH: J_{\mathbf g}(\mathbf x)] is the Jacobian of [MATH: \mathbf g.]

Content:
In other words, we have

Content:
[MATH: \bigg(\substack{\Large \text{Gradient of} \[3pt] \Large\text{composition}}\bigg)
= \bigg(\substack{\Large \text{Jacobian of} \[3pt] \Large\text{the inner function}}\bigg)^T
\cdot \:\:
\bigg(\substack{\Large \text{Gradient of} \[3pt] \Large\text{the outer function}}\bigg).]

Content:
Let’s see this in action.
